A study of cultured cortical neurons found that several psychedelics increased dendritic arbor complexity, measured by Sholl-analysis area under the curve and maximum crossings, through increases in dendritic branch number and total arbor length. Effects were seen with tryptamines DMT and psilocin, amphetamines DOI and MDMA, and ergoline LSD; the structurally distinct psychoplastogen DHF also increased complexity. The compounds had limited effects on primary dendrite number and no effect on the length of the longest dendrite. Serotonin and D-amphetamine had little or no effect.

In an eight-point dose-response study measuring dendritic crossings, most tested psychedelics and entactogens were more potent than ketamine. Ketamine had an EC50 of 132 nM; LSD was especially potent, with an EC50 of 0.409 nM and activity extending into the low picomolar range. Ketamine at 10 μM defined the assay’s 100% efficacy benchmark, and vehicle defined 0%. DMT was tested up to 90 μM to approximate brain concentrations following an antidepressant dose in rats.

Ibogaine was the only tested psychedelic with no effect on neuritogenesis in cultured cortical neurons. Its metabolite noribogaine robustly increased dendritic arbor complexity, with an EC50 comparable to ketamine, supporting the possibility that noribogaine is the active compound in vivo.

In Drosophila larvae, LSD and DOI increased branching of class I sensory neurons whether treatment began in the first instar or late second instar; neither increased total dendritic arbor length. The effect was smaller when treatment began later, possibly because of developmental-stage sensitivity or shorter treatment duration. Chronic exposure to compounds for six days in zebrafish embryos produced no detected differences in head size or statistically significant activity levels. The findings indicate neuronal structural effects across vertebrate and invertebrate species.
